case.case_title: Vinayagamoorthy Attorney-at-Law (on behalf of Wimalenthiran) v. The Army Commander and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. 26/94, decided on 25 November 1996

clause.text: No person shall be arrested except according to law and must be informed of the reason.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the arrest of Wimalenthiran was made according to procedure established by law and whether he was informed of the reason for his arrest as required by Article 13(1).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that Wimalenthiran was arrested without reasonable grounds of suspicion, was not informed of the reasons for his arrest, and the arrest was not in accordance with the procedure established by law.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents claimed that Wimalenthiran was arrested at a checkpoint on 23 October 1993 with reasonable grounds for suspecting him to be involved in offences under Emergency Regulations and that he was informed of the reasons for his arrest.
key_facts: Wimalenthiran was arrested on 2 October 1993 (petitioner) or 23 October 1993 (respondents).
He was blindfolded and detained at secret locations including a building behind the Indian High Commission and Panagoda Army Camp.
No reasonable grounds for suspicion existed at the time of arrest according to the Court.
He was not informed of the reasons for his arrest.
The arresting officer lacked evidence or reasonable grounds to justify the arrest.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that Article 13(1) requires that no person be arrested except according to procedure established by law and that the person arrested must be informed of the reason for the arrest. Reasonable grounds for suspicion must exist at the time of arrest, not based on speculative or vague suspicions.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the arresting officer had no reasonable grounds for suspecting Wimalenthiran of an offence at the time of arrest. The arrest was based on vague suspicion hoping evidence would later justify it. Consequently, the arrest was not in accordance with the procedure established by law and violated Article 13(1). Wimalenthiran was also not informed of the reasons for his arrest.
principles_established: Arrest must be based on reasonable grounds of suspicion at the time of arrest.
Vague or speculative suspicion is insufficient to comply with Article 13(1).
The arrested person must be informed of the reasons for arrest.
Detention orders must specify grounds to enable the detainee to challenge the detention.
precedents_cited: Peiris and Others v. Attorney-General (1994) 1 Sri L.R. 1
Kumara v. Rohan Fernando and Others S.C. Application 22/90

outcome.holding: The Court declared that the arrest of Wimalenthiran violated Article 13(1) of the Constitution because it was not made according to procedure established by law and he was not informed of the reasons for his arrest.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay compensation and costs to Wimalenthiran.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 13(1) was central to the Court's reasoning as it directly governs the legality of arrest and the requirement to inform the arrested person of the reasons, which were both violated in this case.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found no evidence that the arresting officer had reasonable grounds for suspicion at the time of arrest and that Wimalenthiran was not informed of the reasons for his arrest, violating Article 13(1).
